kicker: Qwen3.8-27B throughput claims, one GPU each

scenes.text: Seven hundred, a thousand, sixteen hundred tokens a second on one graphics card. How fast does one person actually read?
scenes.say: Seven hundred, a thousand, sixteen hundred tokens a second, each on one graphics card. So how fast does one person actually read?

scenes.headline: How one GPU serves many streams at once
scenes.sub: Qwen3.8-27B: the total tok/s versus what one user sees
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Tolliver! This week three posts put Qwen three point eight on one card at hundreds of tokens a second. Every one of them is a sum over streams. Let's see why.

scenes.title: One read, many streams
scenes.sub: Why a decode step barely notices a bigger batch
scenes.say: Chapter one. One read, many streams.

steps.say: Every decode step streams all the weights from memory into the chip. With one user, that read is almost the whole cost, and the math units sit waiting.
Put eight streams in the same step. The weights are still read once. Each stream only adds one more row of math, which the card had spare.
Each stream does bring its own memory: a recurrent state of about a hundred and fifty megabytes, plus its KV cache.
One step, eight tokens out. The total climbs nearly eightfold, while each user's speed barely moves.

scenes.title: The whole trick, in one line

parts.note: streams, times tokens each keeps per step
parts.say: The total is the number of streams, times the tokens each one keeps per step.

parts.note: weight reads or math, whichever is slower
parts.say: Divided by the step time, which is the weight read, or the math, whichever takes longer.

scenes.say: Per stream, drop the B. That is the number a person feels.

steps.say: Here it is measured, by one serving stack on one three-oh-ninety: forty-six tokens a second for one stream, three hundred and twenty-one for eight.
Eight users get seven times the total, and each still sees about forty a second.

steps.term: Compute bound: math, not memory, sets the pace
steps.say: Past the mid thirties, the math catches up with the memory. At sixty-four streams the total passes a thousand, and each user gets about sixteen.

scenes.title: What each stream costs
scenes.sub: A hybrid model pays for state before cache
scenes.say: Chapter two. What each stream costs.

scenes.title: One stream's memory, from the config

steps.say: Forty-eight of the sixty-four layers are Gated DeltaNet. Each keeps a fixed matrix per head, a hundred twenty-eight by a hundred twenty-eight.

steps.term: Recurrent state: fixed memory per stream
steps.say: That is about a hundred and fifty megabytes per stream in full precision, read and written on every step, before a single token of cache.
The sixteen attention layers add a KV cache: about thirty-three kilobytes per token in eight-bit floats.
On the three-oh-ninety, that state capped the batch: only thirty-seven of sixty-four requests ever ran.
Halve the state to sixteen bits, and about seventy short requests fit.

scenes.title: Where speculation fits
scenes.sub: Drafts and streams spend the same arithmetic

scenes.title: Eight lanes through one verify pass

steps.say: The five-oh-ninety runs this week split one coding prompt into eight lanes, each writing its own part of one file.
Inside the pass, every lane brings a row for its own next token.

steps.term: Draft: a cheap guess the model verifies
steps.say: And each lane brings draft rows: guesses the big model checks in the same pass, keeping the ones it agrees with.
Every row costs arithmetic. Batching and drafting draw on the same budget, which is why drafting wins below about eight users and batching wins above.
Eight lanes with drafts is the sweet spot where both still pay.
TensorFold's seven hundred is this line: eight parallel code lanes, seven hundred sixty-four tokens a second of decode, summed.
End to end it is six hundred sixty-five. Per lane, about ninety-five.
The sixteen hundred came from Cinference's author, who called it a magic trick. The big counter is the fastest single second.
The run itself averaged one thousand and ninety-nine. Like for like, that is one point four times TensorFold, not twice.

scenes.title: Tokens a second per stream
scenes.say: Divide each total by its streams. About ninety-five a lane, about a hundred and thirty-seven, and about sixteen for each of sixty-four users.

steps.say: The project's demo shows its sixty-four at once: short requests, a hundred twenty-eight tokens in and five hundred twelve out.
It is a fine backend for a pipeline. Its own guide sends chat users to the single-user mode.

scenes.title: What the headlines leave out
scenes.say: The totals are real. Three things shrink them.

items.say: With eight thousand token prompts, eight streams gave about two point four times one stream, not seven.
Lanes finish at different times, so the end of a run has fewer streams decoding.

items.text: A best second is not a run
items.say: And a fastest second is not an average.

scenes.text: Ask how many streams first. Divide the total by them: that is the speed a person feels.
scenes.say: So ask how many streams first. Divide the total by them, and that is the speed a person actually feels.

recap: Weights are read once per step
Each stream adds state and KV
Divide by streams for real speed
scenes.say: Weights are read once per step. Each stream adds its own state. And to know the speed, divide by the streams.
